source.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods Converge Faster with Over-Parameterization (and you can do a line-search)
source.authors: Sharan Vaswani; Frederik Kunstner; I. Laradji; S. Meng; M. Schmidt; Simon Lacoste-Julien

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including supplementary material, is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: Reports adaptive optimizer results on image classification with deep networks, extending optimizer and generalization comparisons to this setting; its experiments do not directly test the claim's random-label memorization result.
record.gate_note: The study reports test/validation accuracy for adaptive methods and SGD variants, and compares training loss and generalization in deep-network experiments. The convex logistic-regression and LIBSVM experiments report training loss only. It does not test random-label fitting or compare architectures, model widths, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example removal.
record.test_reason: The deep-network experiments directly compare held-out accuracy of adaptive optimizers and SGD using stochastic line-search, bearing on V4's dependence on the optimization recipe. They do not reproduce the original limited-tuning comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that step-size adaptation substantially improves empirical performance and that AdaGrad and AMSGrad with line-search can generalize better than SGD on the tested deep-network tasks. Their convergence guarantees concern smooth convex objectives under stated assumptions, rather than generalization guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: Uses adaptive optimizers equipped with stochastic line-search or Polyak step-sizes, and compares them with SGD using line-search and tuned Adam. It does not test the optimizer generalization comparison as framed in the original studies' tuning conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: Step-size strongly affects training performance; line-search variants improve performance. Heavy-ball momentum is sensitive to γ. Deep-network experiments use batch size 128; β is set to 0.9 for AMSGrad, γ = 0.25 found by grid-search for its heavy-ball variant, and Adam step-size is grid-searched.

fits_no_version.finding: Adam, RAdam and AdaBound generalize worse than the proposed adaptive SLS methods in the recorded comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out performance differs among adaptive optimizers and their step-size recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: AMSGrad momentum improves performance relative to no momentum; heavy-ball momentum has a minor, sometimes detrimental effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Momentum formulation affects the performance of adaptive optimizers with line-search.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing factorization rank improves training-loss convergence in synthetic deep matrix factorization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Over-parameterization can improve optimization convergence; these training-loss results do not measure V2's held-out generalization effect.

record.problems: Deep-network results are mainly presented in plots without exact accuracy values or uncertainty estimates. The reported comparison combines optimizer and step-size adaptation, so it does not isolate optimizer effects. Dataset and model coverage is a subset of the larger set described; other results are deferred to the appendix.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Convex logistic-regression and LIBSVM results in Figures 1 and 2 report training loss rather than held-out generalization, so they do not furnish rows for V4.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus random-label training and held-out accuracy under the same architectures and recipes.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
The original limited-tuning regime; language benchmarks; systematic broader hyperparameter tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching from Adam to SGD; and word-level language-model exceptions.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that remove a large-batch penalty.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, and interactions with augmentation and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps relative to competing measures.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

missing.what: Additional held-out optimizer comparisons for CIFAR-10/DenseNet121, Imagewoof/ResNet18 and Imagenette/ResNet18. Captions report consistently strong adaptive SLS performance, but the record omits these conditions. Extract each adaptive-versus-SGD comparison separately.

MNIST validation-accuracy comparisons among adaptive optimizers and SGD with SLS. The supplied text preserves axes and legends but not readable curve identities or values, so the direction cannot be determined.

The authors state that tuned constant-step-size SGD is consistently outperformed by SGD with SLS. This omitted textual comparison helps establish the importance of the SGD baseline recipe; no numerical results or plots are supplied.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V4. Reversed row states describe the direction relative to the adaptive-worse tendency; the verdict is limits_scope because the tested line-search recipe differs from the original limited-tuning regime. Exact accuracy differences and uncertainty cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and held-out performance on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and resulting test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Language benchmarks, limited tuning of only learning rates and decay schedules, broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching from Adam to SGD, and word-level language models.
Large versus small batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations to the recipe.
Dropout additions/removal, training set size regimes, and interaction with weight decay and augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, competing generalization measures, and correlations with generalization gaps.
Influence-based removal of memorized examples and resulting test-accuracy changes.

rows.subject: SGD with SLS
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers using stochastic line-search; compared validation accuracy with adaptive optimizers.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.value: Often competitive with AdaGrad and AMSGrad with Armijo SLS; figure shows curves
rows.note: Authors say adaptive SLS variants consistently have the best performance in generalization, while SGD with SLS is often competitive. Exact points are plotted.
rows.check: Use AdaGrad/AMSGrad with Armijo SLS as the explicit comparison. The authors report better generalization for these adaptive methods, while SGD with SLS is often competitive. Split the aggregate into dataset/model comparisons; Figure 3 covers CIFAR-10/ResNet34, CIFAR-100/DenseNet121, CIFAR-100/ResNet34 and Tiny ImageNet/ResNet18.

rows.subject: Adam
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers with tuned Adam, with step-size selected by grid search.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.value: Worse test performance than AdaGrad and AMSGrad variants with Armijo SLS; curves shown
rows.note: This comparison does not isolate optimizer choice from the line-search step-size adaptation.
rows.check: The recorded comparison is Adam versus other adaptive methods, not versus SGD. It cannot establish V4's adaptive-versus-SGD effect. Recover the SGD comparison from the figure before using this row for V4.

rows.subject: RAdam
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers with RAdam and compared validation performance.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.value: Worse test performance than AdaGrad and AMSGrad variants with Armijo SLS; curves shown
rows.note: Authors report considerably better test performance for the SLS adaptive variants than Adam and RAdam.
rows.check: The recorded comparison is RAdam versus other adaptive methods, not versus SGD; it does not establish V4's effect.

rows.subject: AdaBound
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers with AdaBound and compared training loss and validation accuracy.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.value: Does not generalize as well as AdaGrad and AMSGrad with Armijo SLS; curves shown
rows.note: The paper states AdaBound has comparable training-loss convergence but worse generalization.
rows.check: Comparable training convergence and worse generalization refer to comparison with the proposed adaptive SLS methods. The recorded value does not establish an AdaBound-versus-SGD difference.

rows.subject: AdaGrad + Armijo SLS
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers with AdaGrad equipped with Armijo stochastic line-search.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.baseline: SGD with SLS, Adam, RAdam and AdaBound comparisons
rows.value: Consistently among the best test performance; curves shown
rows.note: Authors report these adaptive variants generalize better than SGD with SLS in the shown deep-network experiments.
rows.check: Replace partial with reversed for the reported adaptive-versus-SGD direction: the authors explicitly report better generalization with suitable step-size adaptation. Separate the SGD comparison from comparisons against adaptive baselines and split dataset/model conditions.

rows.subject: AMSGrad + Armijo SLS
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers with AMSGrad equipped with Armijo stochastic line-search.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.baseline: SGD with SLS, Adam, RAdam and AdaBound comparisons
rows.value: Consistently among the best test performance; curves shown
rows.note: AMSGrad with Armijo SLS is reported to have considerably better test performance than Adam and RAdam. The paper says SGD with SLS is often competitive.
rows.check: Replace partial with reversed for the reported adaptive-versus-SGD direction. The authors report better generalization with suitable step-size adaptation, while SGD with SLS is often competitive. Split dataset/model conditions.

rows.subject: AMSGrad + Armijo SLS + heavy-ball momentum
rows.operation_detail: Trained deep image classifiers using AMSGrad with Armijo SLS and heavy-ball momentum.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; models shown in Fig. 3

rows.value: AMSGrad momentum is consistently better than the heavy-ball variant
rows.note: Comparison is between momentum formulations within the authors' proposed adaptive line-search approach.
rows.check: This compares momentum formulations within an adaptive optimizer, without a recorded SGD accuracy contrast. The subject should be described as the heavy-ball variant of preconditioned updates, replacing AMSGrad momentum rather than adding another momentum term.

rows.subject: AMSGrad + Armijo SLS without momentum
rows.operation_detail: Ablated AMSGrad momentum in deep-network image classification.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet; Figure 11

rows.baseline: AMSGrad with Armijo SLS and momentum
rows.note: The paper reports this as an ablation result; plotted values are not stated numerically.
rows.check: This momentum ablation does not record the adaptive-versus-SGD comparison required for V4. Its aggregate performance statement also does not isolate validation accuracy by dataset/model.

relationships.condition: Image classification with AdaGrad or AMSGrad using Armijo SLS versus SGD using SLS, batch size 128
relationships.reason: R1, R5 and R6 record the authors' explicit finding that adaptive SLS methods can generalize better than SGD, with SGD often competitive; this qualifies the optimizer disadvantage by step-size recipe, without challenging the original limited-tuning result.
relationships.display_finding: Reported generalization advantages for adaptive line-search methods remain unverified, with SGD also described as often competitive.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Deep image classification experiments with batch size 128 and the tested SLS/tuned-Adam recipes
reader_labels.reason: Adaptive methods equipped with Armijo SLS have the strongest reported generalization, but SGD with SLS is often competitive; this does not establish that adaptive optimizers generally generalize worse. Rows R1–R7.
